title: Short Stuff: The wAve
summary: Short Stuff episode on the wave, the stadium crowd action in which fans stand, raise their arms, and sit in sequence. The hosts discuss the hosts' personal feelings about doing the wave, then the disputed invention between "Crazy" George Henderson (Oakland A's game, October 15, 1981, with a Colorado Rockies NHL cheerleading background) and Rob Weller (Washington cheerleader, "expandable cheer," Halloween 1981 game, with band director Bill Bissell suggesting sending it outward). Bissell disputes Henderson's version, saying it was not a true oval and was just a stand-up cheer. The episode covers the wave spreading in the mid-1980s, its local variants, its international name the "Mexican Wave" from the 1986 World Cup in Mexico, a 2002 Hungarian Academy of Sciences study published in Nature (about 20 to 30 people can start a wave, rolling clockwise at about 20 seats per second), etiquette on when not to start one, and anti-wave movements such as Stopthewave.net and a 2022 Texas Rangers scoreboard message.
topics: Hungarian Academy of Sciences wave study

segments.title: Opening
segments.summary: Josh welcomes listeners to Short Stuff and introduces the topic of the wave.

segments.title: What the wave is and the hosts' feelings about it
segments.summary: Chuck describes the stadium wave as fans standing and raising their arms in sequence around the stands. Josh praises the wave and says it has declined, citing a 1984 Michigan Stadium video. Chuck says he participates only halfheartedly and will fully join in for his daughter's sake. They note the Cubs game at Wrigley Field had no wave.

segments.title: Crazy George Henderson's claim
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the dispute over who invented the wave. Chuck describes Crazy George Henderson, a San Jose State cheerleader and freelance pro cheerleader, performing a section-by-section version at an Oakland A's game against the Yankees on October 15, 1981. Josh notes the footage looks wave-like at moments; they call it a proto wave.

segments.title: Henderson's Colorado Rockies history
segments.summary: Henderson says he started developing the wave earlier as a cheerleader for the Colorado Rockies NHL franchise in Denver in the late 1970s, but few fans attended and little was filmed. The Oakland game was the first he documented on camera and posted online. Chuck clarifies that the Rockies were an NHL team then, later becoming the New Jersey Devils.

segments.title: Rob Weller and the expandable cheer
segments.summary: Rob Weller, a University of Washington cheerleader from Tacoma who later hosted Entertainment Tonight, is introduced as the second claimant. He called his version the expandable cheer, which initially moved bottom to top. At a Halloween 1981 game, band director Bill Bissell suggested sending it outward, and Weller adopted that idea to start the wave.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: A short break is announced before the discussion of the dispute.

segments.title: Bissell disputes Henderson's claim
segments.summary: Bissell argues the Henderson wave was not a true oval because it happened in a baseball stadium with a diamond shape, though Chuck counters that waves can occur in square rooms. Bissell also says the Henderson version was just a stand-up cheer section by section. Bissell's harsh remark about Henderson in the press is mentioned.

segments.title: Spread of the wave and local variations
segments.summary: By the mid-1980s the wave had spread to stadiums with local names and variations, such as the silent wave at Michigan Stadium, car key jingling, and waves that met in the middle. Crowds began to see it as disruptive. The hosts say the wave spread from the US to Mexico and became known outside the US as the Mexican Wave, which was showcased at the 1986 World Cup in Mexico.

segments.title: Science of the wave and when to start one
segments.summary: Chuck describes a 2002 study by physicists from the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, published in Nature, that modeled waves using distance between fans, number of visible neighbors, and readiness to stand. The study found about twenty or thirty people are enough to start a wave, which typically rolls clockwise at about twenty seats per second. The hosts discuss that waves are poorly timed at critical moments of a game.

segments.title: Failed waves and standing ovations
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the awkwardness of a failed wave attempt and compare it to a lone standing ovation. Chuck mentions comedian Gary Gulman's joke about standing ovations.

segments.title: Anti-wave movements and closing views
segments.summary: Some fans and announcers oppose the wave as distracting or inappropriate for dull or lopsided games. Stopthewave.net is mentioned, and the Texas Rangers scoreboard message in 2022 warned about pulled muscles. Rob Weller reportedly considered a stop-the-wave campaign but decided people still enjoy it. Chuck says he prefers keeping the wave and criticizes tomahawk chops by the Atlanta Braves, Kansas City Chiefs, and Florida State Seminoles.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh closes Short Stuff, and an iHeartRadio production credit runs.
